Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Explanation

The application is setting the server port. To migrate a Java application that sets the server port to Azure Container Apps:

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java 21 Spring Boot application providing a public photo gallery and authenticated upload/delete operations. The architecture below reflects the checked-in source and deployment configuration, not a verified running deployment; credential values are omitted.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Web browser - Bootstrap 5.3.0 and JavaScript"] end subgraph App["Application Layer - Spring Boot 3.5.0 on Java 21"] Security["Spring Security - stateless HTTP Basic"] Web["Spring MVC - HTTP port 8080"] Views["Thymeleaf templates and static assets"] Business["Photo management and upload validation"] Images["Java ImageIO - image dimensions"] end subgraph Data["Data Access Layer"] ORM["Spring Data JPA and Hibernate"] JDBC["Oracle JDBC driver"] end subgraph Storage["Persistent Storage"] Oracle[("Oracle Database XE 21.3.0 - photos and BLOBs")] Volume[("Docker volume - oracle_data")] end subgraph External["External Services"] CDN["jsDelivr - Bootstrap CSS and JavaScript"] end Browser -->|"HTTP gallery, image and mutation requests"| Security Security -->|"Public reads or authenticated writes"| Web Web -->|"Render gallery and detail pages"| Views Views -->|"HTML, CSS and JavaScript responses"| Browser Web -->|"Upload, browse, navigate and delete photos"| Business Business -->|"Read image headers and limit pixel count"| Images Business -->|"Transactional persistence and retrieval"| ORM ORM -->|"Entity CRUD and native Oracle SQL"| JDBC JDBC -->|"SQL and binary photo data over TCP 1521"| Oracle Oracle -->|"Database files"| Volume Browser -->|"HTTPS asset requests"| CDN Web -->|"JSON upload results and binary image responses"| Browser

Technology Stack Summary

LayerTechnologyVersionPurpose
RuntimeJava / Eclipse Temurin21Executable JAR runtime; container uses a JRE image
ApplicationSpring Boot3.5.0Auto-configuration, dependency injection and embedded servlet hosting
PresentationSpring MVC and ThymeleafManaged by Spring Boot 3.5.0Gallery/detail HTML, multipart upload endpoint and image responses
BrowserBootstrap and plain JavaScript Fetch APIBootstrap 5.3.0; JavaScript unspecifiedResponsive UI, drag-and-drop upload and dynamic gallery updates
SecuritySpring Security and BCryptManaged by Spring Boot 3.5.0HTTP Basic authentication using an in-memory administrator account
Business logicSpring transactions and Java ImageIOBoot-managed transactions; Java 21 ImageIOUpload validation, dimension extraction, navigation and transactional photo operations
PersistenceSpring Data JPA, Hibernate and Oracle JDBC ojdbc8Managed by Spring Boot 3.5.0Entity mapping, repository CRUD and Oracle-specific native queries
DatabaseOracle Database Express EditionCompose image tag 21.3.0-xeStores photo metadata and binary image contents
Build and deploymentMaven, Docker multi-stage build and Docker ComposeBuild image Maven 3.9.9; Docker/Compose versions unspecifiedBuild executable JAR and run application/database containers
Test-only storageH2Managed by Spring Boot 3.5.0Test-scoped alternative database; not production storage

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle holds both metadata and image bytes in the photos table; Photo.photoData is a JPA LOB. Gallery and detail views reference /photo/{id}, which serves the database-backed bytes rather than an uploaded-file directory. Docker Compose places the application and Oracle on a bridge network, waits for database health before application startup, persists Oracle files in oracle_data, and mounts oracle-init for startup scripts. The default profile targets a local Oracle instance; the Docker profile targets the database service. Both profiles configure spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create, so schema recreation at startup can remove existing photo data despite the persistent database volume. The browser retrieves Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr; no application cache, message broker, object-storage integration or outbound business API is evident.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A layered monolith uses constructor injection: MVC controllers depend on a service interface, whose transactional implementation delegates persistence to a Spring Data repository.
  • Photos and metadata share database storage. Native queries use Oracle constructs including NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE and DUAL, coupling retrieval/navigation to Oracle.
  • Reads are public; POST upload and delete require authentication. Security uses stateless HTTP Basic, an in-memory account and BCrypt with externally supplied administrator credentials; CSRF is disabled. Multipart limits are 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request, with service MIME/size checks and a 40-million-pixel limit when image headers can be read.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous HTTP: Browsers request HTML and binary images; multipart upload returns JSON. Detail-page forms POST deletion requests. Controller calls to PhotoService / PhotoServiceImpl and PhotoRepository are direct in-process method calls, not separate services.
  • Database communication: Spring Data JPA uses JDBC to the database. Compose resolves the static database service hostname through container-network DNS; the local configuration targets a local database host. This is not application service discovery.
  • Upload composition: HomeController processes files sequentially. For a successful UploadResult, it performs a further lookup by ID and adds a metadata projection only if the photo is found. Failed results become failure entries; an absent post-upload lookup adds neither entry. Overall success means at least one successful metadata entry. This is local response composition, not gateway aggregation.
  • Asynchronous communication: No message broker, event bus, pub/sub client, background messaging contract, or gRPC service was found.
  • Resilience and timeouts: No explicit application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback service, HTTP-client timeout, or JDBC operation timeout policy was found. Framework/driver defaults are not declared contract guarantees. Compose process restart behavior is not a request retry policy.
  • Error behavior: Gallery read failures produce an empty gallery; detail read failures redirect home; binary retrieval failures return 500. The upload service converts many validation, file-read, and persistence exceptions into failed results. These catches do not guarantee that transaction-commit errors or the controller's subsequent lookup cannot escape. There is no automatic downstream fallback or retry.
  • Discovery, gateway, and balancing: No service registry, API gateway, inter-service aggregation, or client-side load balancer is configured.
  • Availability: Compose starts the application after the database becomes healthy. Database connectivity and required credentials affect availability. Deployment settings and startup mechanisms belong in configuration-inventory.md; credential values are intentionally omitted here.
  • Authentication and authorization: SecurityConfig implements stateless HTTP Basic authentication and an in-memory user with BCrypt-encoded credentials. POST /upload and /detail/*/delete require authentication. Read-only gallery/detail/photo routes and other requests are permitted by the security rule. Although the configured account has an admin role, these routes use authenticated(), not role-based checks. No JWT, OAuth2, method-level authorization, or explicit CORS policy was found.
  • Transport and CSRF: CSRF protection is explicitly disabled. No application HTTPS listener, enforced TLS redirect, or TLS termination component is configured in the inspected deployment; external TLS cannot be inferred. Clients using Basic authentication require an appropriately secured deployment.

Evidence: controller sources, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java, docker-compose.yml, and application configuration files.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose interpolation → required secret inputs: missing required Oracle/application/admin password inputs stop Compose configuration before containers start.
  2. oracle-db → Oracle initialization and account scripts: the mounted startup directory includes 01-create-user.sh, 02-verify-user.sql, create-user.sh, and healthcheck.sql. Shell scripts require ORACLE_PWD and APP_USER_PASSWORD; create-user.sh includes a fixed sleep 30, not a readiness polling loop.
  3. Database health → application launch: Compose uses an inline SQL*Plus check with application-account environment references. The health check runs every 30s, times out after 10s, allows 15 retries, and has a 180s start period. These are check parameters, not a guaranteed overall database boot deadline.
  4. photoalbum-java-app → healthy oracle-db: depends_on.oracle-db.condition=service_healthy gates container startup. Spring then requires resolvable database/admin settings and a usable database during context initialization. Application failures trigger the configured on-failure restart policy.

No application container health check, readiness probe, Spring Cloud Config retry, discovery-server dependency, or explicit application startup timeout was found. The test profile selects in-memory H2 and does not rely on Compose startup ordering.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  1. An operator supplies the named environment variables, optionally using an ignored local .env patterned after .env.example. No automated retrieval from a secret manager or CI provisioning workflow was found.
  2. Compose requires the three password inputs and binds the Oracle administrative password to ORACLE_PWD. It passes application account settings into Oracle and maps the same application credentials to Spring datasource environment variables.
  3. Oracle startup shell scripts use the administrative connection to create the application account if absent and apply grants. 01-create-user.sh specifies a least-privilege intent without DBA/system-wide ANY grants; the separate legacy create-user.sh also runs from the mounted directory and has a different grant sequence. Existing-account password rotation is not established by the create-if-absent workflow.
  4. Spring consumes datasource credentials and separately injects administrator credentials into an in-memory user-details configuration. SecurityConfig uses a password encoder; this application-side hashing does not encrypt environment variables or the local .env file.

No managed identity, service principal, RBAC-based secret retrieval, Vault/Key Vault path, Jasypt encryption, sealed secret, or Docker secret mount is configured. Secret values are passed as ordinary environment variables; the inventory does not reproduce credential defaults or literals.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared collection of photographs and view individual images with their upload information. Authenticated operators can add multiple photographs and permanently remove existing ones.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with in-process components, not independently deployed domain services.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload photographs and update the gallery

Entry point: A user selects or drops files into the gallery; the browser submits POST /upload.

  1. The browser applies Client upload screening, displays progress, and sends eligible files together.
  2. The security filter applies Mutation authorization before upload handling.
  3. HomeController applies Batch admission, then processes submitted files sequentially through PhotoService.
  4. PhotoService applies Server upload admission and Image dimension admission. It reads original bytes and attempts to obtain dimensions without fully decoding the image.
  5. Accepted content becomes a new Photo and is saved with its display information. Photo metadata integrity applies to the entity. Dimension extraction can degrade according to Optional dimensions.
  6. Each normal service return is an UploadResult. For successful results, HomeController separately reloads the Photo and includes its display information in the success list; failures populate the per-file error list.
  7. HomeController returns a combined outcome under Batch result composition. The browser prepends successful photographs to the gallery and displays individual failure messages. It requests image content separately.
  8. A network failure or non-success HTTP response produces a generic browser upload error. There is no automatic retry or rollback of earlier files.

The batch is designed to permit partial success rather than require all photographs to be accepted together. Some errors outside the service's normal result handling can still abort the request; see transaction and error behavior below.

Sources: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-158, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-106, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184.

Workflow 2: Browse the gallery and navigate full-size photographs

Entry points: A visitor opens GET /, selects a photograph at GET /detail/{id}, and the browser retrieves its content at GET /photo/{id}.

  1. HomeController asks PhotoService for the shared collection under Gallery chronology and renders it. A retrieval error is logged and the page renders an empty collection instead.
  2. DetailController applies Photo lookup outcomes. A found Photo is combined with separate previous-photo and next-photo lookups.
  3. PhotoService applies Chronological navigation; the detail page renders available navigation links and upload information.
  4. The browser requests the original image independently. PhotoFileController looks up the Photo, obtains its stored content, and serves it using the stored media type.
  5. Missing content returns not-found; serving errors return a server error. The page and image requests are separate, so successful page rendering does not guarantee image delivery.

Sources: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:212-229, src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-94.

Workflow 3: Confirm and permanently delete a photograph

Entry point: The detail-page form asks for browser confirmation and submits POST /detail/{id}/delete.

  1. Cancelling the browser confirmation leaves the photograph unchanged. This confirmation is a presentation safeguard, not a server-side approval step.
  2. The security filter applies Mutation authorization.
  3. PhotoService looks up the Photo. If absent, it returns false; otherwise it deletes the stored entity, including its original content.
  4. DetailController sets a success or not-found flash message. Exceptions produce a generic failure flash message.
  5. The controller redirects to the gallery, which reloads the remaining collection.

There is no soft-delete state, recovery workflow, external file cleanup, or compensating business operation.

Sources: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-208.

No scheduled jobs, message listeners, batch commands, or business-state initialization routines were found in src/main/java; the application entry point only starts the application.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend-to-backend service calls, gateways, message brokers, circuit breakers, or cross-context identifiers in the implemented workflows.

  • Upload composition: Browser file content flows to HomeController, PhotoService, and the database. HomeController uses the returned photo identifier to reload each successful Photo and compose display information with per-file failures. The response omits image bytes; the browser subsequently fetches content by that same identifier.
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines the selected Photo with identifiers from two chronological queries. These are separate calls within the same application, not a distributed aggregation.
  • Image delivery: The browser obtains original content from PhotoFileController, using the database-backed Photo as the authoritative source. Cache-busting URLs and no-cache image responses favor freshly retrieved content rather than previously cached copies.
  • Business-relevant degradation: Gallery read failures look like an empty collection; detail failures redirect to the gallery; missing image content returns not-found rather than a placeholder. Upload can proceed without dimensions and can report mixed per-file outcomes. There is no alternative storage source or offline fallback.

Sources: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:39-98, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-58, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86, src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:113-132,176-179.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Admission and integrity

  • Client upload screening: The browser accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP MIME types and files no larger than 10 MiB. It does not check empty files or enforce a file-count limit.
  • Batch admission: A null or empty bound file list returns a bad-request result. HomeController's multipart exception handler also returns a bad-request result with “No files provided,” without distinguishing the underlying multipart failure.
  • Server upload admission: PhotoService compares the lowercased supplied content type against the configured allowlist, rejects files larger than the configured maximum, and rejects zero-length files. Current application profiles allow JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP with a 10 MiB maximum. Multipart configuration additionally limits a request to 50 MB. The configured maximum of ten files per upload is not referenced by the controller, service, or browser code and is not an implemented count rule.
  • Image dimension admission: When an image reader recognizes the content, the first image's width multiplied by height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels. This check uses header dimensions rather than full image decoding.
  • Optional dimensions: An I/O exception while reading content or dimensions rejects the file. Other dimension-extraction exceptions are logged and processing continues; no available reader also permits continuation without dimensions. Supplied MIME type is therefore not equivalent to verified decodable image content.
  • Photo metadata integrity: Entity validation declares a nonblank original filename of at most 255 characters, a nonblank MIME type of at most 50 characters, a positive nonnull size, and a nonnull upload time. These are model constraints, not explicit controller validation. Missing dimensions are allowed.
  • Identity and lifecycle: Creation assigns a new random identifier and current application time. A photograph moves from uploaded candidate to persisted Photo and can later be physically deleted. No approval, moderation, editing, duplicate-content detection, or filename uniqueness rule is implemented.

Sources: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-87, src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30, src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:20-27, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-182, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:31-90.

Composition, ordering, and lookup decisions

  • Batch result composition: The response's success flag is true only when at least one uploaded Photo was successfully reloaded and added to the result. A processed batch normally returns HTTP success even if all files failed admission. If a successful upload's reload is empty, it is included in neither list.
  • Gallery chronology: The gallery is loaded newest first. Newly uploaded cards are prepended in the browser rather than refetching the entire gallery.
  • Chronological navigation: Previous means the first returned photograph strictly older than the current upload time, ordered newest first, with that query limited to ten results. Next means the first strictly newer photograph, ordered oldest first, and excludes timestamps beyond the database's current time. Equal timestamps do not qualify in either direction; no tie-breaking rule is defined.
  • Photo lookup outcomes: Blank or missing detail identifiers redirect to the gallery; detail retrieval exceptions do the same. Blank identifiers, absent records, or absent/empty image content return not-found for image requests; other image-serving exceptions return a server error.
  • Computed display information: Optional dimensions are extracted from image headers; upload dates and human-readable sizes are formatted for presentation. No thumbnails, image resizing, pricing, or aggregate business metrics are computed.

Sources: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:69-97, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:215-229, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86, src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:104-125.

Cross-cutting business behavior

  • Mutation authorization: Upload and deletion require authentication; gallery, detail, and image reads are public. The configured account is assigned an administrator role, but endpoint rules check authentication rather than that role. There are no per-photo ownership checks or separate private collections. Credential values are intentionally omitted.
  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level transaction boundaries; read operations override them as read-only. Each controller-to-service upload call has its own transaction, not one transaction for the whole batch. Metadata reload is another service call. Caught repository save failures become UploadResult failures where possible, but transaction commit/rollback errors can occur after the method returns and escape the controller's per-file loop. A prior file's committed upload is not compensated.
  • Read consistency: Selected-photo and navigation lookups are separate read transactions, so detail composition is not one atomic snapshot of concurrent additions/deletions.
  • Error handling: Retrieval and deletion errors are wrapped as runtime exceptions. Gallery/detail/delete controllers handle them as described above; upload has no controller-wide catch around per-file service calls or reloads. No durable retry queue or dead-letter handling exists.
  • Business logging: Upload acceptance/rejection, deletion, retrieval failures, and image delivery are logged with identifiers or filenames; image delivery also logs a small byte preview. There is no persisted business audit trail, actor attribution, or change history.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The project targets Java 21 and uses Spring Boot parent 3.5.0. This initial 3.5 release and the older Commons IO 2.14.0 pin warrant review against current maintenance releases. The separate security assessment checked affected versions against advisories, not runtime exploitability; dependency presence alone does not establish a reachable vulnerability. The resolved Oracle driver is 23.7.0.25.01 and H2 is 2.3.232; Oracle compatibility with Java 21 and the deployed database still requires compatibility validation, and the ojdbc8 artifact name alone does not establish incompatibility. Framework upgrades must preserve compatibility with the Jakarta-based Spring Boot 3 stack.

Notable Observations

  • The only declared parent is org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-parent:3.5.0 (pom.xml:8–13). No explicit BOM imports or dependency-management overrides are declared; Commons IO alone has an explicit dependency version.
  • The resolved tree includes Logback 1.5.18, SLF4J 2.0.17, Hibernate ORM 6.6.15.Final, and Jackson 2.19.0 as transitive dependencies. These are represented in the full inventory, not added to the 11 direct-declaration count.
  • The JSON starter is a JSON serialization dependency, despite its “Image processing” POM comment. The resolved tree attributes Jackson 2.19.0 to the direct JSON starter; shared or omitted dependency paths are not necessarily repeated in Maven's mediated tree.
  • DevTools is optional but has default compile scope, not runtime scope. The build also declares org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-maven-plugin without an explicit version; it is a build plugin, not an application dependency.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The persistence layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, managed through Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. Oracle stores both photo metadata and binary image content; tests select an H2 in-memory database.

Entity Model

erDiagram %% Photo Album owns the photos entity. photos { string id PK "Java String; UUID; length 36" string original_file_name "Java String; required; length 255" bytes photo_data "Java byte array; nullable LOB" long file_size "Java Long; required" string mime_type "Java String; required; length 50" datetime uploaded_at "Java LocalDateTime; required" int width "Java Integer; nullable" int height "Java Integer; nullable" }

Mapping source: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-82.

  • Photo maps to photos. UUID identifiers and upload timestamps are assigned in its constructor rather than through database-generated identifiers/defaults.
  • A non-unique index, idx_photos_uploaded_at, covers uploaded_at. No additional uniqueness constraint, foreign key, optimistic-lock version field, or entity relationship is declared.
  • There are no association fetch modes, cascades, or bidirectional links to document. photoData is a basic @Lob without an explicit lazy-fetch annotation; custom queries select the binary column alongside metadata.
  • UploadResult is an operation-result model, not a mapped entity.
  • PhotoServiceImpl is class-level transactional. Its list, lookup, and navigation methods override that default with read-only transactions; upload and deletion retain the write transaction default (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,53-54,67-68,216-228).

Key Repository Methods

The sole interface is PhotoRepository extends JpaRepository in src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-62. Standard CRUD, paging, and sorting are inherited; service code uses inherited identifier lookup, save, and delete operations. The table focuses on custom queries.

ServiceRepositoryNotable MethodsPurpose
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native SQL selects all photo columns, including image bytes, newest first. Oracle NVL supplies a MIME fallback. No pagination or metadata-only projection.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedBefore(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Native SQL finds earlier timestamps in descending order; outer Oracle ROWNUM limits results to ten.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedAfter(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Native SQL finds later timestamps in ascending order, capped at Oracle's current database date via SYSDATE/DUAL. No row-count limit.

Timestamp parameters are bound through @Param, not interpolated into SQL. Navigation service methods consume only the first returned entity. No custom cross-service bulk finder, stored-procedure invocation, or separate JDBC/MyBatis data-access path was found.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application and one repository access a single configured database/schema at a time. Oracle and H2 are environment alternatives, not separately owned service stores. Photo metadata and binary content share the photos table; no separate object store or independently persisted user/album model was found.

Controllers access persistence through PhotoService; no cross-service database access, remote data aggregation, schema-per-service split, or cross-service transaction protocol is present. Reads and writes share the same entity, repository, and database connection configuration; there is no separate CQRS read model. No tenant/user ownership column or row-level ownership predicate is mapped.
